peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What unexpected scent did Kostya notice amid the smoke and burnt flesh?
options: Strong alcohol
Burning rubber
Women’s perfume
Wet earth
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: the stench of burnt flesh, of smoke from the fires… and women’s perfume

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What did the two mirrors in Kostya’s hideout allow him to see?
options: Both entrances without showing himself
The stairwell and the roof
The whole office floor at once
The avenue without leaving the barricade
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: Two mirrors, angled in the corners so that he could see both entrances without showing himself

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: Which feature had Kostya learned to use especially to recognize the lizard-like aliens?
options: Their hands
Their voices
Their shadows
Their eyes
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: most of all — the eyes

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: How long was the first warning broadcast that appeared on television screens around Earth?
options: Two minutes
One hour
Half an hour
Five minutes
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: a brief, two-minute broadcast

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What was Kostya doing when he missed Free Will’s first broadcast?
options: Hiding in the office tower
At a shooting competition
On patrol with his squad
Traveling between cities
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: Kostya was at a shooting competition at the time and missed the broadcast entirely.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: According to Free Will’s second broadcast, what did the invaders feed on by taking over human bodies?
options: Electricity, metals, and chemical fuel
Human consciousness, emotion, and life-force
Human blood, organs, and body heat
Memories, dreams, and spoken language
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: they fed on human consciousness, emotion, and life-force.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What did Free Will say could reveal aliens disguised as humans?
options: Their odd behavior when their true nature slipped through
A particular smell that followed them everywhere
Their inability to speak any human language
A mark that appeared on their skin at night
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: they could be recognized by their odd behavior.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: In Taka’s report to Thorg, what fraction of the planet’s surface did he say was uninhabitable?
options: One-third
Three-quarters
One-half
Two-thirds
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: After the use of the most powerful weapons, two-thirds of the surface is uninhabitable.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What was the sik, and how was the treatise stored inside it?
options: A medical instrument containing samples in a sealed chamber
A weapon component holding a recording in a crystal core
A data-storage cylinder containing information encoded in a bacterium’s DNA
A navigation device containing a map etched onto its surface
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: a small cylindrical object used for data storage — a sik. Inside, encoded in the DNA of a specially bred bacterium

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What name did Taka imagine taking if he earned three new symbols?
options: Takargkh
Taka-Thorg
Thorgak
Takargh
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: Takargkh — it had a fine ring to it

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: According to the Council Chairman, what had happened to Taka before he attacked Thorg?
options: He had been sent to Earth as a prisoner
He had been ordered to sabotage the scout ship
He had stolen a weapon from the Council
He had been infected by a parasitic organism
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: The younger, named Taka, was infected by the parasitic organism and attacked the elder, Thorg.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What unusual weather does Kostya encounter at the end, despite the time of year?
options: Large flakes of snow falling in the middle of July
Hail falling under a clear sky in March
A warm rain falling in the middle of January
Dust storms sweeping through the city in October
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: From the sky, large flakes of snow began to fall. Something was definitely wrong with the world — it was the middle of July.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What does the perfume most strongly suggest about the girl, beyond Kostya’s suspicion that she is an alien?
options: It may be a last connection to her former human life
It proves she has recently joined Kostya’s resistance group
It identifies her as a member of the Free Will organization
It shows she is trying to lure Kostya away from the tower
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: or perhaps it was her final link to the past.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: How does Free Will’s campaign help bring about the planetary disaster?
options: It disables communication systems before the aliens arrive
It convinces people to evacuate the cities and abandon the planet
It persuades governments to surrender their weapons to the invaders
It spreads distrust that turns populations and forces against one another
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: A bit of study, a carefully crafted provocation, and the natives would annihilate themselves.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What is the central irony in the Council’s response to the warning about the invasion?
options: It assumes the scout ship survived even though the recording says it did not
It welcomes the invasion because it believes the planet is still intact
It blames humanity for the conflict while refusing to examine the recording
Its members begin to fear infiltrators and militias much as humanity did
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: there are rumors of people’s militias forming, hunting down ‘invaders,’ and spreading an alien recording with translation.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What most clearly motivates Thorg to keep Taka’s research for himself?
options: He plans to use the research to restore Earth’s energy systems
He wants to protect Taka from being punished for the invasion
He believes the treatise is too dangerous to share with anyone
He hopes to gain status in the Council by claiming the discovery
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: Thorg, conqueror of worlds, would become a member of the Council of Aggressors — perhaps even its leader. The death of insignificant Taka would go unnoticed.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: Why does Taka reach for the blaster after asking to record new data onto the sik?
options: He believes the weapon will help him escape the damaged scout ship
He intends to destroy the control panel before the ship can land
Thorg’s refusal convinces him the elder will keep the research from him
Thorg has openly ordered him to defend himself against an attack
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: Now there was no doubt — Thorg would never let his research leave his claws. The younger’s hand reached for the blaster

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: How does the story connect the human conflict on Earth with the later crisis facing the Council?
options: Both societies become consumed by suspicion of infiltrators and threats within
Both societies unite under a single leader to resist an outside invasion
Both societies stop using weapons after receiving warnings from scouts
Both societies discover that their governments have already defeated the enemy
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: Members of the Council of Aggressors looked around at one another with suspicion — as though seeing each other for the first time.

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What does Kostya’s thought about shooting practice suggest about his survival?
options: He regrets practicing because it caused him to lose his comrades
A skill he once questioned has become useful in the ruined world
His shooting skill has convinced him to abandon the resistance
His training has made him certain that the war is nearly over
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: So there was the answer to his wife’s old question: What good is all that stupid shooting practice?

peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.question: What is the effect of ending with Kostya heading toward gunfire as snow falls in July?
options: It shows that Kostya has decided to leave the city and avoid the war
It suggests that the fighting has ended and Kostya can return home
It shows that the world has suffered catastrophe, but Kostya continues the fight
It reveals that the snow is a sign the alien invasion has been defeated
peculiarities-of-planetary-conquest.evidence: But life went on. He had to find his people and fight the enemy.

the-nose.question: What date is given for the strange occurrence in St Petersburg?
options: The 7th April, 18--
The 25th April, 18--
The 25th March, 18--
The 24th March, 18--
the-nose.evidence: On the 25th March, 18--, a very strange occurrence took place in St Petersburg.

the-nose.question: What was the only inscription on Ivan Jakovlevitch’s sign-board?
options: Coffee and bread sold here.
Razors sharpened here.
Shaving done here daily.
Blood-letting done here.
the-nose.evidence: the only inscription to be read was, "Blood-letting done here."

the-nose.question: What did Ivan Jakovlevitch say he wanted for breakfast?
options: Coffee with two onions.
A loaf with salt and butter.
Fresh-baked bread with coffee.
A fresh loaf with onions.
the-nose.evidence: To-day, Prasskovna Ossipovna, I do not want any coffee; I should like a fresh loaf with onions.

the-nose.question: Whose nose did Ivan Jakovlevitch recognize in the loaf?
options: The porter’s, whom he shaved every Tuesday and Saturday.
Kovaloff’s, whom he shaved every Sunday and Wednesday.
The police inspector’s, whom he shaved every Monday and Friday.
The doctor’s, whom he shaved every Thursday and Sunday.
the-nose.evidence: he saw at once that this nose could belong to no other than to Kovaloff, a member of the Municipal Committee whom he shaved every Sunday and Wednesday.

the-nose.question: What did the sentry say after Ivan Jakovlevitch let the wrapped nose drop?
options: Stop there! You have lost your parcel!
Take care! You have let your cloth fall!
Look out! You have let something drop!
Come back! You have dropped your bread!
the-nose.evidence: Look out! You have let something drop!

the-nose.question: What sort of position had Kovaloff come to St Petersburg hoping to obtain?
options: A police superintendency, though he would accept a barber’s post.
A vice-governorship, though he would accept a bailiff’s post.
A state-councillorship, though he would accept a porter’s post.
A committee chairmanship, though he would accept a doctor’s post.
the-nose.evidence: He had come to St Petersburg with the view of obtaining some position corresponding to his rank, if possible that of vice-governor of a province; but he was prepared to be content with that of a bailiff in some department or other.

the-nose.question: What rank did the nose’s uniform and plumed hat appear to indicate?
options: Police inspector.
Caucasian committee-man.
Municipal committee-man.
State-councillor.
the-nose.evidence: The hat, adorned with a plume, showed that it held the rank of a state-councillor.

the-nose.question: How did the nose explain why it could not have a close relation with Kovaloff?
options: Their seals showed they belonged to different districts.
Their uniform buttons showed they belonged to different departments.
Their passports showed they served different provinces.
Their hats showed they held different ranks in the same department.
the-nose.evidence: To judge by the buttons of your uniform, you must be in quite a different department to mine.

the-nose.question: Why did the advertisement official say he could not publish Kovaloff’s notice?
options: He feared the paper might be compromised by such an advertisement.
He said the paper had no room for notices about officials.
He required Kovaloff to bring the nose in person first.
He believed the notice would reveal Kovaloff’s private address.
the-nose.evidence: Because it might compromise the paper.

the-nose.question: Why did Kovaloff suspect Madame Podtotchina of causing his misfortune?
options: He thought she wanted revenge because he had avoided marrying her daughter.
He thought she wanted revenge because he had reported her to the police.
He thought she wanted his position after he refused to recommend her son.
He thought she wanted revenge because he had refused to pay her a debt.
the-nose.evidence: This must be the reason why the lady, in revenge, had resolved to bring him into disgrace

the-nose.question: Where was the nose headed when the police official arrested it?
options: It was getting into a carriage for Riga.
It was entering a shop in the Tauris Gardens.
It was boarding a boat for the Isaac Bridge.
It was getting into a carriage for Moscow.
the-nose.evidence: It has just been found. It has been arrested just as it was getting into a carriage for Riga.

the-nose.question: What did Ivan Jakovlevitch do to shave Kovaloff after the nose returned?
options: He used the razor without touching Kovaloff’s face at all.
He braced his thumb against Kovaloff’s lower jaw and cheek.
He held the nose in place with a cloth under Kovaloff’s chin.
He shaved only the cheeks and left the chin untouched.
the-nose.evidence: by placing his wrinkled thumb against the Major's lower jaw and cheek

the-nose.question: Why does Kovaloff find the loss of his nose especially devastating?
options: He believes that losing it will prevent him from returning to his former home.
He fears that he will no longer be able to recognize his friends in the street.
He depends on his nose to perform his work as a barber and shave his customers.
He believes his appearance and social standing are essential to his ambitions and connections.
the-nose.evidence: I go into good society, and this evening I am invited to two parties.

the-nose.question: What is most strongly suggested by the nose’s independent identity and higher official rank?
options: The story makes social rank seem absurdly powerful, even when separated from the person it supposedly belongs to.
The nose has been promoted because it has proved more honest than Kovaloff.
Kovaloff’s earlier service in the Caucasus has made the nose a legitimate official.
The nose is secretly obeying Kovaloff’s orders while trying to protect his career.
the-nose.evidence: There you are wrong, respected sir; I am myself. Besides, there can be no close relations between us.

the-nose.question: How do Ivan Jakovlevitch and Kovaloff respond differently to the missing nose?
options: Ivan seeks help from the authorities, while Kovaloff decides to hide it from everyone.
Ivan mainly fears being punished for possessing it, while Kovaloff mainly fears the damage to his appearance and status.
Ivan tries to claim it as his own, while Kovaloff refuses to admit that it has disappeared.
Ivan treats it as a joke, while Kovaloff assumes it is a punishment for his drinking.
the-nose.evidence: The thought that the police might find him in unlawful possession of a nose and arrest him, robbed him of all presence of mind.

the-nose.question: What does the advertisement-office episode contribute to the story’s portrayal of officialdom?
options: The official treats an extraordinary real crisis as an implausible joke and worries about the paper’s reputation.
The official offers to publish the notice if Kovaloff pays an unusually large fee.
The official immediately believes Kovaloff and organizes a search through the city.
The official recognizes the nose as a government official and refuses to interfere.
the-nose.evidence: I see that you are a witty man, and like to have your little joke.

the-nose.question: What does Kovaloff’s suspicion of Madame Podtotchina reveal about his thinking?
options: He has firm evidence that she hired the barber to steal the nose.
He suspects her because she wants to prevent him from accepting a government position.
He has always believed her daughter is conspiring with the police against him.
He interprets the strange event through his own marriage negotiations and assumes it is personal revenge.
the-nose.evidence: He himself paid her court readily, but always avoided coming to the point.

the-nose.question: What is the effect of the city’s rumors and crowds surrounding the nose?
options: They persuade Kovaloff to give up searching and leave St Petersburg.
They prove that the nose deliberately visits the places named in every rumor.
They show how quickly an extraordinary event becomes public spectacle, gossip, and an opportunity for profit.
They cause the authorities to explain how the nose became an official.
the-nose.evidence: A certain speculator with a grave, whiskered face ... invited the public to stand on them and look in, at the modest charge of twenty-four kopecks.

the-nose.question: What does the abrupt return of the nose to Kovaloff’s face suggest about the story’s strange events?
options: They are resolved without a rational explanation, preserving the story’s deliberately improbable quality.
They follow a medical treatment that gradually restores Kovaloff’s face.
They are revealed to have been a dream caused by Kovaloff’s illness.
They are explained as a trick arranged by Madame Podtotchina and the barber.
the-nose.evidence: The same nose which had masqueraded as a state-councillor ... was found one morning in its proper place

the-nose.question: How does the narrator’s ending frame the tale’s improbability?
options: The narrator concludes that the nose’s adventures were a warning against public officials.
The narrator insists that every event has a clear scientific explanation.
The narrator apologizes for inventing the story and says it never happened.
The narrator questions the point of such a story but still allows that rare strange events can occur.
the-nose.evidence: such cases do occur--rarely, it is true, but now and then actually.

rip-van-winkle.question: What happened to the Kaatskill Mountains when the rest of the landscape was cloudless?
options: They turned blue and purple beneath a crown of bright stars.
They disappeared behind a curtain of rain that covered the river.
They reflected the green of the nearby fields across their slopes.
They gathered grey vapours around their summits, which glowed in the setting sun.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: they will gather a hood of grey vapours about their summits, which, in the last rays of the setting sun, will glow and light up like a crown of glory.

rip-van-winkle.question: When was the Dutch village founded, according to the narrator?
options: During the first years of Peter Stuyvesant’s government.
During the reign of King George the Third.
When Hendrick Hudson first explored the river.
After the revolutionary war had ended.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: having been founded by some of the Dutch colonists in the early times of the province, just about the beginning of the government of the good Peter Stuyvesant

rip-van-winkle.question: Which earlier event had Rip’s Van Winkle ancestors taken part in?
options: They joined Hendrick Hudson on the voyage up the river.
They accompanied Peter Stuyvesant to the siege of Fort Christina.
They fought at the storming of Stony Point.
They helped establish the village inn under King George.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: accompanied him to the siege of Fort Christina.

rip-van-winkle.question: What did Rip do for the village children?
options: He took them fishing and taught them to repair the village fences.
He brought them to the inn and showed them how to play ninepins.
He made their playthings and taught them to fly kites and shoot marbles.
He taught them to read old newspapers and debate public events.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: He assisted at their sports, made their playthings, taught them to fly kites and shoot marbles

rip-van-winkle.question: What did Rip do when fishing, even if he received no encouragement?
options: He moved from pond to pond until he caught a trout.
He gave up after an hour and went to help a neighbour.
He borrowed a lighter rod and fished from the riverbank.
He sat fishing all day without a single nibble.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: he would sit on a wet rock, with a rod as long and heavy as a Tartar’s lance, and fish all day without a murmur, even though he should not be encouraged by a single nibble.

rip-van-winkle.question: What did Wolf do when Dame Van Winkle flourished a broomstick or ladle?
options: He fled to the door, yelping.
He ran out to the village inn.
He stood his ground beside the fireplace.
He hid beneath Rip’s chair and growled.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: at the least flourish of a broomstick or ladle he would fly to the door with yelping precipitation.

rip-van-winkle.question: How did Nicholas Vedder show that he approved of something?
options: He stood up and moved into the sunlight beneath the tree.
He sent out short, angry puffs of smoke.
He spoke at length and tapped his pipe against the bench.
He took his pipe from his mouth and gravely nodded.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: taking the pipe from his mouth, and letting the fragrant vapour curl about his nose, would gravely nod his head in token of perfect approbation.

rip-van-winkle.question: What was the strange old man carrying when he met Rip in the mountains?
options: A stout keg that seemed full of liquor.
A wooden box packed with old Dutch clothes.
A rusted firelock wrapped in a cloth.
A heavy sack filled with mountain herbs.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: He bore on his shoulder a stout keg, that seemed full of liquor

rip-van-winkle.question: What did Rip find beside him when he awoke on the mountain?
options: A hunting knife with a handle carved from oak.
An old firelock with a rusty barrel and a worm-eaten stock.
A clean, well-oiled fowling-piece with a broken strap.
A keg of liquor with a flagon resting beside it.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: he found an old firelock lying by him, the barrel incrusted with rust, the lock falling off, and the stock worm-eaten.

rip-van-winkle.question: What name was painted beneath the altered portrait over the inn door?
options: NICHOLAS VEDDER
GENERAL WASHINGTON
PETER STUYVESANT
THE UNION HOTEL
rip-van-winkle.evidence: underneath was painted in large characters, “GENERAL WASHINGTON.”

rip-van-winkle.question: What did Judith Gardenier say had happened to her mother?
options: She had moved in with Judith after the old house fell into decay.
She had died after breaking a blood vessel in a fit of passion at a New-England pedler.
She had died of a fever shortly after Rip went to the mountains.
She had left the village after Rip disappeared and never returned.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: she broke a blood vessel in a fit of passion at a New-England pedler.

rip-van-winkle.question: According to the postscript, what happened when a hunter dropped one of the gourds near Garden Rock?
options: A great stream burst out and swept him down the precipices.
A bear sprang from the rocks and chased him to the Hudson.
The gourd split open and scattered seeds across the lake.
A storm cloud formed and drove him back into the forest.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: he let it fall among the rocks, when a great stream gushed forth, which washed him away and swept him down precipices

rip-van-winkle.question: What most clearly explains why Rip is popular with the villagers despite neglecting his own farm?
options: He is a stern but fair husband who keeps order among the village families.
He is a skilled farmer who regularly shares his harvest with the village.
He is a respected public speaker who leads the village’s political discussions.
He is generous with his time and companionship, helping neighbours and entertaining children.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: Rip was ready to attend to anybody’s business but his own

rip-van-winkle.question: Why does Rip ultimately wander into the mountains?
options: He is trying to escape both the work of his farm and his wife’s constant scolding.
He is searching for a missing neighbour who has gone hunting.
He has been sent to deliver a keg of liquor to the men at the inn.
He is hoping to find a new route to the village across the mountains.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: his only alternative, to escape from the labour of the farm and clamour of his wife, was to take gun in hand and stroll away into the woods.

rip-van-winkle.question: What is the main effect of Rip’s long sleep on his return to the village?
options: It convinces him that his old neighbours have deliberately hidden from him.
It makes him confront a transformed community and a span of history he has missed.
It allows him to escape the village’s political arguments for only a few days.
It gives him a new ambition to restore his neglected farm and family home.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: the whole twenty years had seemed to him as but one night.

rip-van-winkle.question: How does the change from Vedder’s inn to the Union Hotel reflect the village’s transformation?
options: The village has abandoned elections and returned to the rule of its old landlord.
The quiet colonial gathering place has become a busier, politically contentious public world.
A place for newspapers and debate has become a centre for farming and trade.
A prosperous Dutch inn has become a private home for Rip’s descendants.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: There was a busy, bustling, disputatious tone about it, instead of the accustomed phlegm and drowsy tranquillity.

rip-van-winkle.question: How is Rip’s identity crisis resolved?
options: The man in the cocked hat discovers Rip’s name on his old gun.
Rip recognizes himself in the younger man leaning against a tree.
Nicholas Vedder returns and identifies Rip at the village inn.
His daughter’s recognition and the villagers’ memories confirm who he is.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: The name of the child, the air of the mother, the tone of her voice, all awakened a train of recollections in his mind.

rip-van-winkle.question: What matters most to Rip about the end of British rule and the changes in government?
options: He blames the revolution for his long sleep and demands his farm back.
He is largely indifferent to political change but delights in escaping his wife’s control.
He eagerly embraces politics and becomes a leader in the new republic.
He mourns the king’s departure more than the loss of his home and friends.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: the changes of states and empires made but little impression on him; but there was one species of despotism under which he had long groaned, and that was--petticoat government.

rip-van-winkle.question: What role does the narrator’s note play in the story’s presentation of Rip’s experience?
options: It reveals that Rip invented his story to explain why he left the village.
It admits that the narrator has no evidence and considers the story a local joke.
It explains that the mountain episode was borrowed directly from a German legend.
It frames the tale as an extraordinary event the narrator claims to believe and support with testimony.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: I have even talked with Rip Van Winkle myself

rip-van-winkle.question: How does the postscript connect the local legends to the events of Rip’s story?
options: It argues that the old stories are false and that Rip’s sleep had an ordinary cause.
It identifies the old squaw spirit as the person who gave Rip the liquor.
It presents the Catskills as a place of spirits and marvels, making supernatural mountain events part of local tradition.
It explains that the villagers invented the mountain spirits to protect the local hunting grounds.
rip-van-winkle.evidence: The Kaatsberg or Catskill mountains have always been a region full of fable.

a-christmas-carol.question: What did C. D. hope the Ghost of an Idea would do to readers?
options: Haunt their houses pleasantly without making them ill-tempered
Make them curious about the spirits of their ancestors
Encourage them to give money to the poor
Remind them to keep Christmas with their families
a-christmas-carol.evidence: May it haunt their houses pleasantly

a-christmas-carol.question: What does Scrooge’s nephew’s defense of Christmas reveal about his view of the holiday?
options: He believes its chief benefit is that it brings wealth to people who celebrate it
He values it as a time when people show kindness and recognize their shared humanity
He regards it as a solemn religious observance that should be kept privately
He sees it mainly as a chance to escape work and enjoy a large meal
a-christmas-carol.evidence: a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time

a-christmas-carol.question: Who signed the register of Marley’s burial?
options: The clerk, Scrooge, the chief mourner, and the parish beadle
The undertaker, the clerk, two witnesses, and Scrooge
The clergyman, Scrooge, the undertaker, and Marley’s nephew
The clergyman, the clerk, the undertaker, and the chief mourner
a-christmas-carol.evidence: The register of his burial was signed by the clergyman, the clerk, the undertaker, and the chief mourner.

a-christmas-carol.question: What made the clerk’s fire look like only one coal?
options: Scrooge had ordered the clerk to let the fire die before closing time
The coal delivery had been delayed by the weather outside
Scrooge kept the coal-box in his own room, so the clerk could not replenish it
The clerk had used most of the coal to heat the water for his tea
a-christmas-carol.evidence: the clerk's fire was so very much smaller that it looked like one coal.

a-christmas-carol.question: How does the nephew’s behavior toward Scrooge contrast with Scrooge’s attitude toward him?
options: The nephew challenges Scrooge because he hopes to take over the business
The nephew stops visiting because Scrooge has insulted his wife
The nephew continues to offer friendship despite Scrooge’s repeated rejection
The nephew pretends to be cheerful so that Scrooge will lend him money
a-christmas-carol.evidence: His nephew left the room without an angry word, notwithstanding.

a-christmas-carol.question: What objects made up the chain Marley wore?
options: Cash-boxes, chains, silver spoons, papers, keys, and money bags
Ledgers, contracts, scales, coins, padlocks, and iron bars
Locks, watches, coins, account books, rings, and iron weights
Cash-boxes, keys, padlocks, ledgers, deeds, and heavy purses
a-christmas-carol.evidence: it was made (for Scrooge observed it closely) of cash-boxes, keys, padlocks, ledgers, deeds, and heavy purses wrought in steel.

a-christmas-carol.question: What is the central meaning of the chain Marley forged in life?
options: His failure to leave money to Scrooge has trapped him in an unfinished partnership
His success in business has made him responsible for managing the wealth of the dead
His selfish choices have bound him to remorse and to the consequences of neglecting others
His fear of poverty has prevented him from finding peace in the afterlife
a-christmas-carol.evidence: I wear the chain I forged in life

a-christmas-carol.question: What did the Ghost of Christmas Past hold, despite the wintry appearance of its clothing?
options: A small lantern trimmed with summer flowers
A sprig of mistletoe tied with a white ribbon
A branch of fresh green holly
A candle set in a silver holder
a-christmas-carol.evidence: It held a branch of fresh green holly in its hand

a-christmas-carol.question: What reason did Fan give for bringing Scrooge home from school?

Their mother had arranged for Scrooge to begin an apprenticeship

His dislike of Christmas began because his family refused to celebrate it

Old Joe
Dick Wilkins

Their affection and gratitude make their celebration joyful despite their poverty
Their poverty prevents them from enjoying Christmas until Scrooge helps them
Their simple meal matters less to them than the chance to impress their neighbors

Poverty and Hunger

His watch, his coat, and the silver candlesticks from the bedside table

A basket of fruit and chestnuts from the grocer
A goose from the baker’s shop near the corner

He would provide Bob’s family with a new house and clothing

Weight
Duration

The Provincial Mayor
Filby
The Psychologist

A pair of tattered, blood-stained socks
A pair of slippers, one of them torn
A pair of muddy boots with broken laces

A quartz rod had cracked and needed replacing.

The year Eight Hundred and Twenty Thousand Seven Hundred and One, A.D.
The year Eight Hundred and Two Thousand Seven Hundred and Ten, A.D.

A sour fruit with a thick, yellow skin
A floury fruit in a three-sided husk
A small red fruit with a cluster of hard seeds

the-time-machine.question: Why did the Time Traveller first become acquainted with Weena?

He rescued her from Morlocks while she was exploring a ruined building.

It twisted around and trapped his foot against the shaft.

the-time-machine.question: Where did the Time Traveller find a box of matches in the Palace of Green Porcelain?

In an air-tight case in a gallery of technical chemistry
Inside a drawer beneath a table in the mineral gallery
Under a broken floor tile in the museum’s central hall

The fire went out almost immediately in the damp undergrowth.

A broken matchbox found in the laboratory
A page of drawings covered in moss
A bent brass rail from the Time Machine
the-time-machine.evidence: I have by me, for my comfort, two strange white flowers

the-time-machine.question: What is the Time Traveller’s central argument for treating time as a dimension like space?
options: A body must endure for some time to exist, and consciousness moves along time in one direction.
Time differs from space because it has length but no measurable direction.
People can move through time freely, but habit prevents them from noticing it.

They suspect his cleverness and whim make his apparent frankness hard to trust.
They think the Psychologist has hypnotised them into misremembering the event.

the-time-machine.evidence: Afterwards I found I had got only a half truth—or only a glimpse of one facet of the truth.

Separate ways of life could eventually divide humanity into distinct kinds of people.
The wealthy and the workers would become physically identical through intermarriage.
Class divisions would disappear once industry moved underground.
the-time-machine.evidence: the gradual widening of the present merely temporary and social difference between the Capitalist and the Labourer was the key to the whole position.

the-time-machine.question: How do the discoveries about the Morlocks change the apparent relationship between the two future peoples?
options: The Eloi are no longer secure masters; they have become vulnerable to the Morlocks.
The Morlocks are shown to be harmless servants who fear the Eloi’s intelligence.
The Eloi control the Underworld but refuse to let the Morlocks live above ground.
The two peoples have formed a cooperative society in which each protects the other.
the-time-machine.evidence: The Eloi, like the Carlovignan kings, had decayed to a mere beautiful futility. They still possessed the earth on sufferance

the-time-machine.question: What does Weena’s relationship with the Time Traveller reveal about his response to the future world?

Her gifts persuade him to abandon his investigations and remain permanently with the Eloi.
Her intelligence teaches him how to operate the machine and return to his own time.
Her fear convinces him that the Eloi are secretly plotting against him.
the-time-machine.evidence: the little doll of a creature presently gave my return to the neighbourhood of the White Sphinx almost the feeling of coming home

the-time-machine.question: What principle does the Time Traveller draw from the Eloi’s decline?
options: Security encourages people to develop new skills even when no problems remain.
Art and beauty inevitably preserve a people’s strength and independence.
A society becomes more intelligent as it eliminates every form of physical labor.
Intelligence and adaptability depend on encountering change, danger, and need.
the-time-machine.evidence: There is no intelligence where there is no change and no need of change.

the-time-machine.question: What do the narrator’s final thoughts about the flowers suggest about the story’s ending?
options: The flowers show that Weena was able to follow the Time Traveller into his own time.
Even amid human decline and uncertainty, tenderness and gratitude may survive.
The flowers prove that the Time Traveller’s account was only a carefully planned trick.
The narrator believes the future will certainly restore humanity to its former greatness.
the-time-machine.evidence: even when mind and strength had gone, gratitude and a mutual tenderness still lived on in the heart of man.
